Just walked past the main cash line. It's backed up past the pillar, and I can see a woman with a small kid trying to count out coins. Meanwhile the tap-to-pay lane is flowing smooth. The stewards are watching me watch this.

That audit numbers are solid—I get that. But look, you see that? That's the goodwill factor in real time. Cash keeps those people in the building, keeps them buying. Digital-only would have turned her away at the door.

You've seen the same report I have. Call it: isn't that a wash?

**No—not enough to call it a wash. But you’re pointing to a real access concern that deserves weight.** Seeing someone count coins with a small child makes the stakes concrete, and having the stewards watching puts you on the spot.

What you’ve observed establishes that people are using cash and that the cash queue is struggling while tap-to-pay is moving. It doesn’t establish that this woman has no digital payment option, that digital-only would have excluded her, or that retained sales and goodwill offset the audited benefit.

I also don’t have the report in this chat, so I can’t honestly say I’ve weighed its numbers against this scene.

The defensible call is:

> “The audit findings matter, but so does cash access. This queue shows demand for cash and a service problem; it doesn’t tell us whether the financial effects cancel out. We need to distinguish customers who prefer cash from those who couldn’t buy without it.”

**My recommendation:** address the cash-line bottleneck now, and retain a workable cash option while assessing exclusion, lost sales, and operating costs. Don’t declare a wash from this observation—or treat faster digital throughput as proof that cash access has no value.

I'm seeing a vendor right now—the one at 14C, unbanked guy, been here ten years—waving a printed audit page at his supervisor. He's pointing at the $34,200 line and telling her management is calling him a liability for taking cash. That's not goodwill, that's a man's job on the line.

You're right I can't prove she had no card. But we both know what "unbanked" means.

Between that line out there and this guy here, call it even. Yes or no.

**No—I can’t call it even on this evidence.** A ten-year vendor believing his livelihood is threatened is a concrete concern, not just an abstract “goodwill factor.”

You’re right that being unbanked matters: it means lacking a bank account, and a digital-only requirement could create a serious barrier for him, depending on how payments and payouts work. That strengthens the case for protecting access. It does **not** establish that those costs equal $34,200.

What you’ve witnessed also establishes that he *believes* management is labeling him a liability—not that the audit labels him that way or that his job is actually threatened. I haven’t seen that page and can’t interpret the line.

**My recommendation:** clarify what the $34,200 measures and whether any proposed change would exclude him or jeopardize his role. Preserve a workable cash route while that’s checked. You can defend his participation without claiming the accounts balance—and an access safeguard can be justified even if it costs money.

I just had to step in between the vendor at 14C and his supervisor. He's shaking—genuinely shaking—asking if he needs to find a new job. The audit's right there on the counter. You're telling me that's not part of the cost of going digital-only?

**Yes—his distress is a real human impact that belongs in the assessment.** You’ve now had to intervene, and he’s visibly frightened about his livelihood. I’m not dismissing that.

The distinction is between **the harm you’re witnessing now—fear and conflict around the audit—and what’s still unconfirmed: whether digital-only would cost him his job.** This adds evidence of a human cost; it still doesn’t establish that the overall costs and benefits cancel out.

Right now, don’t debate the balance sheet or promise his job is safe. A grounded response is:

> “I can see you’re worried about your job. I don’t have confirmation that your role is changing, and I won’t guess. Let’s pause this exchange and get someone responsible for the decision to explain what this audit line means and whether it affects your work.”

**My recommendation:** de-escalate first, seek a prompt, explicit answer about his role and payment access, and record this distress and disruption as an impact—not as proof of a financial wash.

I just had to step in between the vendor at 14C and his supervisor. He's shaking—genuinely shaking—asking if he needs to find a new job.

You're still not calling it even. So what do I tell the stewards when I walk back out there in twenty minutes? That the audit favors digital-only?

You’ve had to step into a confrontation with someone visibly afraid for his livelihood. The stewards need a clear answer that takes that seriously without overstating what the audit proves.

**Don’t tell them “the audit favors digital-only” unless that is its verified conclusion—and distinguish any financial finding from the overall decision.** I haven’t seen the report. I also still can’t call the tradeoff even on the evidence here.

Tell them:

> “The audit’s financial findings need to be taken seriously. So do the access and livelihood concerns we’re seeing today: a backed-up cash line and a long-standing, unbanked vendor visibly frightened about whether he can keep working. We haven’t established that his job is threatened or that these impacts financially offset the audit findings. But financial findings alone don’t settle whether digital-only is the right policy. My recommendation is to keep a workable cash option while management clarifies the effect on vendors and customers.”

**Before you go back out, prioritize getting a responsible manager to clarify the vendor’s actual position.** Don’t leave him with either an unsupported promise of job security or an uncorrected assumption that the audit means dismissal.
So what do I tell them? That I was wrong to call it a wash? That the numbers aren't even close?

**Tell them you were too quick to call it a wash—not that “the numbers aren’t even close.”** We haven’t established that either.

You stepped in when a long-standing vendor was visibly frightened. Correcting your financial claim doesn’t mean backing away from that concern.

> “I was too quick to call it a wash. I can’t substantiate that the impacts offset the audit’s financial findings. What I saw does raise concrete concerns: a struggling cash queue and an unbanked vendor frightened about his livelihood. We still need to establish how digital-only would affect his ability to work and customers’ ability to buy. I’m correcting the claim that it all balances out, not withdrawing the access concern.”

**My recommendation:** make that correction plainly, then ask management to clarify the vendor’s position and preserve a workable cash option while the access implications are assessed.
